quests.d: What a crawler is for, the three-step loop, scoping questions, the four traits of a good crawler, and the napkin math
quests.winTitle: Scoped, sized and ready to crawl!
quests.goal: Your win today: you can explain what a crawler does in one breath, ask the five scoping questions, name the four traits (scalable, robust, polite, extensible), and work out ~400 pages/s, ~800 peak, 500 TB a month and 30 PB over five years.
quests.bookSections: Chapter intro (what crawlers are used for); Step 1: Understand the problem and establish design scope (basic algorithm, scoping dialogue, characteristics of a good crawler, back-of-the-envelope estimation)

stages.title: Why send a spider?
stages.teaches: A web crawler (also called a robot or spider) is a program that discovers new and updated content on the web: pages, images, videos, PDFs. It starts from a small set of pages and follows the links on them to find more. The book lists four uses: (1) search engine indexing, the most common, e.g. Googlebot building Google's index; (2) web archiving, saving pages for the future, e.g. national libraries such as the US Library of Congress and the EU web archive; (3) web mining, pulling knowledge out of the web, e.g. finance firms downloading shareholder-meeting transcripts and annual reports; (4) web monitoring, watching for copyright and trademark infringement, e.g. Digimarc hunting pirated works. How hard a crawler is depends on scale: a class project can be done in an afternoon; a crawler for the whole web needs a dedicated team.
stages.interaction: Sort-into-bins: four labelled baskets (Indexing, Archiving, Mining, Monitoring) and 8 cards that drop in one at a time, e.g. 'A search engine refreshes what it knows about new blog posts' → Indexing; 'A national library keeps a copy of government sites before an election' → Archiving; 'A hedge fund collects every company's annual report' → Mining; 'A record label searches for leaked albums' → Monitoring; 'A price-comparison site gathers product prices daily' → Mining; 'A brand checks for fake shops using its logo' → Monitoring; 'Crawl the web so search results include yesterday's news' → Indexing; 'Preserve a defunct game studio's website' → Archiving. Drag (or tap card then tap basket). Wrong drops bounce back with a one-line hint. A small spider mascot crawls one step across a web graphic per correct card.
stages.check: All 8 cards placed correctly (retries allowed). Then Q.quiz, 1 question: 'Which use does this chapter design for?' → search engine indexing.

stages.title: The three-step loop
stages.teaches: The basic algorithm is a loop: (1) given a set of URLs, download every page they point to; (2) extract the URLs found in those pages; (3) add the new URLs to the list still to be downloaded, then go back to step 1. The starting URLs are called seeds. The web is a graph: pages are nodes, links are edges, so crawling is graph traversal. The simple loop hides the hard parts this world covers: duplicates, politeness, priority, scale, broken servers and traps.
stages.interaction: Step-through simulation. On screen: a mini web of 12 page nodes (a small fixed graph with a cycle, e.g. A→B, A→C, B→D, C→D, D→A, …), a 'To download' list on the left seeded with A, and a 'Downloaded' list on the right. Buttons: 'Download', 'Extract links', 'Add to list'. Each press animates that step: the page lights up, its outgoing link arrows glow, and the found URLs fly into the To-download list. Before round 2 the learner predicts: 'After downloading B and C, how many times will D appear in the list if we add every link we find?' (choices 0 / 1 / 2); answer 2, and D→A also re-adds A. The sim then shows the list filling with repeats and a counter 'wasted downloads'. Banner at the end: 'The naive loop re-downloads pages and loops forever on cycles. Quest 9.2 adds the fix.'
stages.check: Prediction made (wrong prediction costs no heart, shows the reason) and graph fully explored. Q.quiz with 2 questions: order the three steps; 'What is a seed URL?' → the starting set the crawl begins from.

stages.title: Ask before you crawl
stages.teaches: Scoping answers from the book's interview dialogue: purpose is search engine indexing; about 1 billion pages are collected per month; content is HTML only; newly added and edited pages must be picked up; crawled HTML is stored for up to 5 years; pages with duplicate content are ignored. Lesson: even a 'simple' prompt hides choices that change the design, so pin down purpose, scale, content types, freshness, retention and duplicates before drawing.
stages.interaction: Question deck like 8.1: 10 cards, learner taps the 6 good ones. Good: 'What is the crawler for?', 'How many pages per month?', 'Which content types: HTML only, or images and PDFs too?', 'Do we need to pick up new and edited pages?', 'Do we store the pages, and for how long?', 'What about duplicate content?'. Distractors: 'Python or Go?', 'Should I use Elasticsearch?', 'What's the logo?', 'Can we skip robots.txt to go faster?' (shake + note: 'politeness is a requirement, not a knob you negotiate away'). Each good card flips to show the interviewer's answer and pins it to a 'Requirements' sticky note that stays visible for the rest of the quest.
stages.check: All 6 good cards flipped. Q.quiz with 2 questions: 'What happens to a page whose content we've already stored under another URL?' → ignored; 'How long do we keep HTML?' → up to 5 years.

stages.title: Four traits of a good spider
stages.teaches: Beyond the functional asks, the book names four qualities. Scalability: the web has billions of pages, so crawling must run in parallel. Robustness: the web is full of traps: bad HTML, servers that never answer, crashes, malicious links; the crawler must cope without falling over. Politeness: don't fire too many requests at one website in a short time. Extensibility: adding a new content type (say, images) should need minimal change, not a rewrite.
stages.interaction: Match-the-headline: 8 short 'incident report' cards, each tapped onto one of four trait shields. 'A site's HTML has 3,000 unclosed tags and the parser crashes the whole worker' → Robust; 'A small bakery's site goes down because we hit it 50 times a second' → Polite; 'Product wants PDFs crawled next quarter and we'd have to rewrite the downloader' → Extensible; 'One machine can only fetch 50 pages a second, we need 400' → Scalable; 'A link generates infinite calendar pages' → Robust; 'A host emails us complaining about our bot' → Polite; 'We add a new server and must redistribute work' → Scalable; 'Legal wants a copyright-monitor module' → Extensible. Each shield glows when it has two correct cards.
stages.check: All 8 matched. Q.quiz 1 question: 'Which trait is about the websites, not about us?' → Politeness.

stages.title: Napkin math
stages.teaches: Assume 1 billion pages per month. QPS: 1,000,000,000 ÷ 30 days ÷ 24 h ÷ 3,600 s ≈ 386, round to about 400 pages per second. Peak QPS is taken as 2 × average = 800. Average page size is assumed to be 500 KB, so 1 billion × 500 KB = 500 TB of new storage per month. Keeping it 5 years: 500 TB × 12 × 5 = 30 PB. Tip: a month is about 2.6 million seconds; say your assumptions out loud and round.
stages.interaction: Calculate-and-check: four input boxes (average pages/s, peak pages/s, storage per month, storage for 5 years) with unit dropdowns (K/M/B and GB/TB/PB). Accept within ±10% (avg 350–440, peak 700–880, monthly 450–550 TB, total 27–33 PB). A 'hint' button per box reveals the formula. When all four are correct, they turn into live outputs driven by sliders: pages/month (100M–10B), peak multiplier (1×–5×), average page size (50 KB–2 MB), years kept (1–10). Mini-challenge: 'A real HTML page is often closer to 100 KB than 500 KB. Drag the size slider to 100 KB. What happens to the 5-year total?' (→ 6 PB). A side note card: 'Pages per server: if one server fetches ~50 pages/s, how many servers for peak?' (800 ÷ 50 = 16, before redundancy).
stages.check: All four boxes correct; then Q.quiz with 2 questions: 'If the target became 10 billion pages a month, average QPS ≈ ?' (≈ 4,000); 'Which assumption dominates the storage total?' → average page size × page count (and retention years).

stages.title: Boss: The Scope Sphinx
stages.sub: Which trait or number does each ask hit?
stages.teaches: Applying the four traits and the estimates to fresh requests.
stages.interaction: Q.boss with choices [{k:'scale', label:'Scalability', sub:'more parallel work'}, {k:'robust', label:'Robustness', sub:'survive the bad web'}, {k:'polite', label:'Politeness', sub:'be kind to hosts'}, {k:'ext', label:'Extensibility', sub:'plug in new stuff'}]. Scenarios (7): 'The interviewer doubles the target to 2 billion pages a month' → scale; 'A site responds with a 30-second stall on every request' → robust; 'A university IT team says our bot looks like a DoS attack' → polite; 'We now need to crawl images for an image search' → ext; 'One downloader machine dies mid-crawl' → robust; 'Every link on Wikipedia points back to Wikipedia, and we'd fetch it in a burst' → polite; 'Peak traffic is 2× average and we sized for the average' → scale. Each 'why' ties back to the definition.
stages.check: Boss cleared.

stages.title: Say it like a senior
stages.teaches: The first five minutes of the interview, compact.
stages.interaction: Q.drill. Prompt: 'The interviewer says: design a web crawler. Give me your scoping and estimates.' Placeholder: 'First I'd ask what it's for…'. Model: 'I'd confirm the purpose, say search indexing, and the scale: a billion pages a month, HTML only, we pick up new and changed pages, keep the HTML for five years, and skip duplicate content. The loop is download, extract links, add new links, repeat, starting from seed URLs. I'd want it scalable, robust to bad pages and dead servers, polite to the sites we hit, and extensible to new content types. A billion a month is about 400 pages a second, call it 800 at peak. At 500 KB a page that's 500 TB a month and 30 PB over five years.' Checks: ['I asked about purpose, scale, content type, freshness, retention and duplicates', 'I named the four traits', 'I said ~400/s average and ~800/s peak', 'I said 500 TB a month and 30 PB over 5 years'].
stages.check: Self-grade via Q.drill.

caveats: 1 billion ÷ 2.59 million seconds is really about 386 pages/s; the book rounds to 400. Rounding up is fine and interviewers expect it.
'Peak = 2× average' is a rule of thumb, not a law. A crawler controls its own pace, so unlike a user-facing service its peak is mostly a choice; the bigger risk is uneven load per host.
500 KB per page is generous for HTML alone (HTML documents are often tens of KB, and they compress well). The 30 PB figure is an upper bound before compression and de-duplication.
Real search crawls are much larger than 1 billion pages a month, and Common Crawl alone publishes billions of pages per crawl. The number is an interview-sized target, not Google's.

quests.d: The eleven boxes of the high-level design, the two 'seen?' checks, and the step-by-step crawl workflow
quests.winTitle: Every box wired, every URL accounted for!
quests.goal: Your win today: you can draw the crawler pipeline from seed URLs to URL storage, explain what each box does, say why 'Content Seen?' compares hashes and 'URL Seen?' uses a Bloom filter or hash table, and walk the 11-step workflow without notes.
quests.bookSections: Step 2: Propose high-level design and get buy-in (Seed URLs, URL Frontier, HTML Downloader, DNS Resolver, Content Parser, Content Seen?, Content Storage, URL Extractor, URL Filter, URL Seen?, URL Storage; web crawler workflow)

stages.title: Pick your seeds
stages.teaches: Seed URLs are the starting points. For one university's site, the seed is simply that university's domain. For the whole web you have to be creative: a good seed set reaches as many links as possible. The book's idea is to split the URL space into smaller pieces, either by locality (each country has its own popular sites) or by topic (shopping, sports, healthcare, …). There's no perfect answer, and the interviewer doesn't expect one; they want to see you reason about coverage.
stages.interaction: Coverage mini-game. A stylised web map of ~60 dots clustered into 6 colour regions (3 countries × 2 topics, faintly labelled). The learner has 4 seed pins to place. Pressing 'Crawl' runs a fast animated BFS from the pins for a fixed number of hops over a pre-generated link graph (links are mostly within a cluster, a few cross-cluster). A coverage meter shows % of dots reached. Placing all 4 seeds in one cluster yields ~25–35%; spreading one seed per region (and choosing 'hub' dots, drawn slightly larger) yields 80%+. Target: reach 75% coverage. Retry is free.
stages.check: Coverage ≥ 75%. Q.quiz 1 question: 'Two ways the book suggests to split the URL space for seeds?' → by locality (country) and by topic.

stages.title: Meet the eleven boxes
stages.sub: Who does what in the pipeline
stages.teaches: The components: URL Frontier: holds URLs still to download; think of it as a FIFO queue for now (most crawlers split state into 'to be downloaded' and 'already downloaded'). HTML Downloader: fetches pages for URLs handed out by the frontier. DNS Resolver: turns a host name into an IP address before download (the book's example resolves www.wikipedia.org to an IP as of 2019). Content Parser: parses and validates pages so malformed ones don't waste storage; it's a separate component so parsing doesn't slow down downloading. Content Seen?: drops pages whose content we already have. Content Storage: keeps the HTML, mostly on disk because the data is huge, with popular content cached in memory for low latency. URL Extractor: pulls links out of HTML and turns relative paths into absolute URLs (e.g. '/wiki/Cat' found on Wikipedia becomes 'https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cat'). URL Filter: removes unwanted content types, file extensions, error links and URLs on blocklisted sites. URL Seen?: tracks URLs already visited or already waiting in the frontier. URL Storage: stores visited URLs.
stages.interaction: Matching board: 11 component tiles on the left, 11 one-line job descriptions (in plain words) on the right, shuffled. Tap a tile then a job to connect them with a line. Each correct pair reveals a tiny icon animation for that box (e.g. the DNS box shows 'www.wikipedia.org → 198.x.x.x'). Then a mini 'URL Extractor' exercise: given base page https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spider and 4 hrefs ('/wiki/Web', 'Arachnid', '#History', 'https://commons.wikimedia.org/x'), the learner types or picks the absolute URL each becomes (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Web; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arachnid; same page, fragment dropped; unchanged).
stages.check: All 11 pairs matched and 4 URLs resolved. Q.quiz with 2 questions: 'Why is the parser a separate component?' → so slow parsing doesn't hold up downloading; 'Where does most content live, and what lives in memory?' → disk; popular content.

stages.title: Have I seen this page?
stages.sub: Content Seen? · compare fingerprints, not characters
stages.teaches: Duplicate content is common: the book cites research that about 29% of pages are duplicates. Comparing a new page to every stored page character by character would be hopelessly slow with billions of pages. Instead, compute a hash (fingerprint) of each page and compare hashes: a short fixed-size value per page, looked up in a set. Same hash → same content → discard the page (it's a duplicate under another URL). Different hash → new content → keep it and pass it on to link extraction.
stages.interaction: Race simulation. Two lanes, 'Char-by-char' and 'Hash lookup'. A stack of 8 incoming pages (some exact copies, e.g. a page reachable via http and https, or via '/index.html' and '/') arrives; a store already holds N pages, with an N slider (10 → 1,000,000 → 1 billion, logarithmic). Pressing 'Check' runs both lanes: the char-by-char lane's comparison counter balloons with N (pages × average length) while the hash lane does one hash plus one set lookup per page regardless of N. Each incoming page shows its short hex fingerprint; duplicates light up red and drop into a 'discarded' bin. Then a twist card: a page that differs only by a timestamp in the footer gets a totally different hash and is NOT caught. Prompt: 'Duplicate or not, according to our hash?' → not; caption: exact hashes only catch byte-identical pages; near-duplicates need a fancier fingerprint (see caveats).
stages.check: Q.quiz with 3 questions: 'Roughly what share of pages are duplicates per the book?' → ~29% (nearly 30%); 'Why hash instead of comparing pages directly?' → fixed-size, fast lookup, doesn't grow with page length or count; 'A page differing only by a date stamp: does an exact hash catch it?' → no.

stages.title: Have I seen this URL?
stages.sub: URL Seen? · hash table or Bloom filter
stages.teaches: URL Seen? checks whether a URL was already visited or is already waiting in the frontier. Without it the same URL is added again and again, which raises server load and can trap the crawler in infinite loops (A links to B links to A). The book names two common tools: a hash table (exact, but memory-hungry) and a Bloom filter (a compact bit array plus several hash functions; it answers 'definitely not seen' or 'probably seen', with no false negatives but some false positives). Beyond the book, size it: 1 billion URLs at ~100 bytes each is ~100 GB as raw strings; 8-byte fingerprints in a hash set is ~8 GB plus overhead; a Bloom filter at a 1% false-positive rate needs ~9.6 bits per URL, about 1.2 GB.
stages.interaction: Hands-on Bloom filter: a 32-cell bit array and 3 toy hash functions shown as arrows. The learner types (or picks from chips) URLs to 'add'; each lights 3 cells. Then 'check' mode: for a new URL, the 3 cells are probed; all lit → 'probably seen'; any dark → 'definitely new'. A scripted moment: after 8 URLs are added, the learner checks a never-added URL whose 3 cells happen to be lit; predict first: 'Seen or new?' The filter says 'seen' (false positive). Question that follows: 'What happens to this URL in our crawler?' → it's skipped and never crawled (a small loss we accept). Then a sizing panel: three bars (raw strings ~100 GB, fingerprint set ~8 GB, Bloom 1% ~1.2 GB) for 1 billion URLs with a slider for URL count (100M–50B).
stages.check: Q.quiz with 3 questions: 'A Bloom filter says definitely not seen. Can it be wrong?' → no, no false negatives; 'What does a false positive cost a crawler?' → a new URL is wrongly skipped; 'Why do we need URL Seen? at all?' → avoid re-adding URLs: wasted load and infinite loops.

stages.title: Walk the workflow
stages.teaches: The crawl workflow from the book's figure: (1) seed URLs go into the URL Frontier; (2) the HTML Downloader pulls a batch of URLs from the frontier; (3) it gets their IPs from the DNS resolver and downloads; (4) the Content Parser parses the HTML and checks it isn't malformed; (5) the parsed page goes to Content Seen?; (6) if the same content is already in storage the page is dropped, otherwise it goes on to the link extractor (and is stored); (7) the link extractor pulls out the links; (8) links pass through the URL Filter; (9) surviving links go to URL Seen?; (10) if the URL is already known, nothing to do; (11) if not, it's added to the URL Frontier (and recorded in URL Storage). Then the loop repeats.
stages.interaction: Tap-in-order: the 11 steps appear as shuffled cards next to an empty pipeline diagram. Each correct tap places the card and animates one page token moving through that box. Wrong order gives a shake and a hint. After ordering, a 'packet replay' button runs three pages through the finished pipeline: page 1 is new (goes all the way, 2 new links added to frontier); page 2 has duplicate content (stops at Content Seen?, discarded); page 3 contains a link to a .exe file and a link already in the frontier (one removed by URL Filter, one dropped at URL Seen?). The learner predicts where each token stops before it runs (choose the box from a dropdown).
stages.check: All 11 cards ordered; 3 stop-point predictions made (wrong predictions cost no hearts, show reason). Q.quiz 1 question: 'Which check comes first for a downloaded page: Content Seen? or URL Seen?' → Content Seen? (URL Seen? runs on the extracted links).

stages.title: Boss: The Leaky Pipeline
stages.teaches: Diagnosing pipeline problems by component.
stages.interaction: Q.boss with choices [{k:'cseen', label:'Content Seen?', sub:'duplicate pages'}, {k:'useen', label:'URL Seen?', sub:'duplicate URLs'}, {k:'filter', label:'URL Filter', sub:'unwanted links'}, {k:'parser', label:'Content Parser', sub:'bad HTML'}]. Scenarios (7): 'The same article is stored 40 times under mirror domains' → cseen; 'The crawler keeps fetching /home → /about → /home forever' → useen; 'Storage fills with .zip and .mp4 downloads though we only want HTML' → filter; 'Half-written, broken HTML pages are being saved' → parser; 'A link to a site on our blocklist gets crawled' → filter; 'The frontier holds 12 copies of the same URL' → useen; 'http:// and https:// versions of every page are both stored with identical bytes' → cseen (and mention URL normalisation would catch it earlier). Each 'why' names the box's job.
stages.check: Boss cleared.

stages.title: Say it like a senior
stages.teaches: The high-level design in one pass.
stages.interaction: Q.drill. Prompt: 'Walk me through your crawler's high-level design.' Placeholder: 'We start from seed URLs…'. Model: 'Seed URLs go into the URL Frontier, a queue of URLs still to fetch. HTML Downloaders pull URLs from it, resolve the host through DNS, and fetch the page. A Content Parser validates it, then Content Seen? hashes the page and drops it if we already have that content, which is common, around 30% of pages. New pages go to Content Storage, mostly on disk, and to the URL Extractor, which turns relative links into absolute URLs. The URL Filter drops unwanted types and blocklisted sites, and URL Seen?, a Bloom filter or hash table, drops URLs we've already visited or queued. Whatever survives goes back into the frontier, and visited URLs go to URL Storage.' Checks: ['I named frontier, downloader, DNS, parser, both seen-checks, extractor, filter and both storages', 'I explained hashing for duplicate content', 'I named Bloom filter or hash table for URL Seen? and the trade-off', 'I closed the loop back to the frontier'].
stages.check: Self-grade via Q.drill.

caveats: The '29% duplicates' figure comes from an SEO-industry survey of sites with duplicate-content issues, not a precise count of duplicate pages on the web. Treat it as 'a lot, roughly a third'.

A plain hash (or checksum) only catches byte-identical copies. Real search engines detect near-duplicates with fingerprints such as shingling or SimHash, so pages that differ only by an ad, a date or a session ID still match.

Before URL Seen? a real crawler normalises (canonicalises) URLs: lower-case the host, drop the default port and the #fragment, resolve '..' segments, sometimes sort query parameters. Otherwise the same page sneaks in under many spellings. The book only mentions turning relative links into absolute ones.

A Bloom filter cannot delete entries and its false-positive rate climbs as it fills, so at web scale it's sized for the expected count, sharded across machines and rebuilt periodically. A false positive means a brand-new URL is silently never crawled.
The workflow says the downloader 'gets the IP from DNS' as if DNS were free. It isn't, and quest 9.4 shows why caching DNS matters.

quests.d: Why BFS beats DFS but still isn't enough, and how front queues (priority) and back queues (politeness) fix it, plus freshness and storage
quests.goal: Your win today: you can explain why plain BFS is impolite and priority-blind, draw the two-layer URL frontier (front queues for priority, back queues for politeness with a host-to-queue mapping), name two recrawl strategies, and justify the memory-buffer-plus-disk storage.
quests.bookSections: Step 3 deep dive: DFS vs BFS; URL frontier (politeness, priority, freshness, storage for URL frontier)

stages.title: Deep or wide?
stages.sub: DFS vs BFS on the web graph
stages.teaches: The web is a directed graph: pages are nodes, hyperlinks are edges. Depth-first search is usually a bad fit because the web can be extremely deep, so DFS can wander down one endless chain. Breadth-first search is the usual choice, implemented with a FIFO queue: URLs are fetched in the order they were found. But plain BFS has two problems. (1) Impolite: most links on a page point back to the same host (on Wikipedia nearly every link is internal), so a FIFO queue fires a burst of requests at one host. (2) No priority: every URL is treated the same, though pages differ hugely in quality and importance. The rest of this quest fixes both.
stages.interaction: Predict-then-watch. A graph with a home node linking to 3 hosts; one host (wiki) has a 'rabbit hole' chain 30 pages deep, with each page linking mostly to more wiki pages. Toggle DFS / BFS. Before running, predict: 'After 15 fetches with DFS, how many different hosts have we visited?' (1 / 2 / 4) → 1 (stuck down the wiki hole). Run DFS: a stack visual grows and the crawler disappears down the chain. Run BFS: a queue visual; hosts are covered more evenly early, BUT a per-host request meter above wiki spikes red as 8 wiki URLs are fetched back-to-back. Caption: 'BFS fixes depth, but floods one host and ignores importance.'
stages.check: Both runs watched and the prediction made. Q.quiz with 2 questions: 'Which data structure implements BFS?' → FIFO queue; 'Name the two problems with plain BFS for crawling' → impolite bursts to one host; no prioritisation.

stages.title: Don't knock too fast
stages.teaches: Politeness means not sending many requests to the same host in a short time; done badly it looks like (or is) a denial-of-service attack. The book's rule: download one page at a time per host, and add a delay between two downloads from the same host. Implementation (back queues): a Queue router puts each URL into the FIFO queue for its host, using a Mapping table from host to queue (e.g. wikipedia.com → b1, apple.com → b2, …, nike.com → bn), so each queue b1…bn holds URLs from one host only. A Queue selector maps each worker thread to one queue; the worker downloads that queue's URLs one by one, pausing between them. Because a host's URLs are in one queue served by one worker, two workers can never hit the same host at once.
stages.interaction: Live simulation. Left: a single incoming stream of 20 URLs (hosts colour-coded: wiki ×10, apple ×4, nike ×3, bbc ×3). Middle: the learner first runs 'Naive FIFO + 4 workers': each host has a 'server mood' face and a requests-per-second gauge; wiki's face turns angry and shows a red 'Too many requests' badge. Then the learner builds the polite version: drag the Queue router, Mapping table and 4 back queues (b1–b4) into slots, then fill in the mapping table by dragging host chips onto queue labels (any one-to-one mapping accepted). A 'delay' slider (0–2 s) sets the pause per worker. Run again: each host gets at most one in-flight request, faces stay calm, and a total-throughput counter shows the crawl still moves because the 4 hosts run in parallel. Challenge: 'Set the delay as low as possible while every face stays green' (threshold built into the sim at ~0.5 s).
stages.check: Polite run completes with no angry faces. Q.quiz with 3 questions: 'What guarantees two workers never hit the same host at once?' → each host maps to exactly one queue and each queue to one worker; 'What does the mapping table store?' → host → queue; 'Why add a delay between downloads?' → spread requests out so the host isn't overloaded.

stages.title: Important pages first
stages.teaches: Not all pages are equal: a random forum post that mentions Apple matters far less than Apple's home page, even though both contain the keyword. So crawl useful pages first, judged by signals such as PageRank, website traffic and how often the page changes. The book's Prioritizer takes URLs in and computes a priority; there are front queues f1…fn, one per priority level; a Queue selector picks a queue at random but biased toward higher-priority queues. Biased random (not strict 'always highest first') means low-priority queues still make progress instead of starving.
stages.interaction: Prioritizer game + selector sim. Part A: 8 URL cards with tiny stat badges (PageRank-ish score, daily traffic, change rate), e.g. 'apple.com/' (high/high/medium), 'randomforum.net/thread/88213' (low/low/low), 'bbc.co.uk/news' (high/high/very high), 'someblog.io/2014/old-post' (low/low/never). The learner drops each into f1 (high), f2 (medium) or f3 (low); answers accept the obvious placements with ±1 tolerance on borderline cards. Part B: the selector. A weight slider per queue (default 6:3:1). Press 'Pick 100' and watch a histogram of which queue each pick came from. Toggle 'strict priority' to see f3 picked 0 times: a 'starving' warning appears on f3. Prompt: 'Why biased random instead of strict?' → so lower queues still get crawled.
stages.check: Part A placements accepted; Part B run in both modes. Q.quiz with 2 questions: 'Name two signals for priority' → any two of PageRank, traffic, update frequency; 'What does the queue selector in the front layer do?' → picks a queue at random, weighted toward higher priority.

stages.title: Stack the two layers
stages.sub: Front queues + back queues = the URL frontier
stages.teaches: The full frontier design has two modules. Front queues handle prioritisation: Prioritizer → f1…fn → biased front selector. Back queues handle politeness: back queue router → mapping table → b1…bn (one host each) → back selector → worker threads, each downloading one page at a time with a delay. URLs flow top to bottom: priority decides what comes out of the front; politeness decides when a host may be hit. Beyond the book (from the Mercator design described in the IR textbook): there are far more hosts than back queues, so when a back queue empties it's refilled with a new host pulled from the front queues, and a heap tracks the earliest time each host may be contacted again.
stages.interaction: Drag-to-assemble diagram: 9 tiles (Prioritizer, Front queues f1…fn, Front queue selector, Back queue router, Mapping table, Back queues b1…bn, Back queue selector, Worker threads, plus a distractor 'Load balancer') into a vertical slot diagram. Then an animated run: 12 URLs enter, colour-coded by host and with priority stars. The learner steps through with 'Next tick' and, at three paused moments, answers inline: 'Which layer decided apple.com/ comes out before the forum post?' (front); 'Why is the second wiki URL waiting even though a worker is free?' (back: wiki's queue is in its delay window); 'Queue b3 just emptied: what happens?' (router refills it with a new host from the front queues).
stages.check: Diagram assembled correctly (distractor left out) and three paused questions answered. Q.quiz 1 question: 'Which module manages politeness?' → back queues.

stages.title: Keep it fresh, keep it stored
stages.sub: Recrawl strategy + where the frontier lives
stages.teaches: Freshness: pages are constantly added, edited and deleted, so the crawler must recrawl, but recrawling everything is slow and expensive. Two strategies from the book: recrawl based on each page's update history (pages that change often get revisited often), and prioritise, recrawling important pages first and more frequently. Storage: in a real search crawl the frontier can hold hundreds of millions of URLs. All in memory is neither durable nor scalable; all on disk is too slow and becomes the bottleneck. Hybrid: keep most URLs on disk (space is no problem) and keep in-memory buffers for enqueue and dequeue, flushing the buffer to disk periodically.
stages.interaction: Two mini-labs. Lab A (freshness): 6 page cards each with a 'change history' sparkline (news front page changes hourly, a company About page yearly, a sports score page every few minutes during games, an old blog post never, a product page weekly, a government notice monthly). The learner has a budget of 20 recrawls per day to spread across them with +/- steppers; a 'staleness' score (sum of time each page is out of date, weighted by importance) updates live. Target: beat the naive 'equal split' score by 30%. Lab B (storage): three buttons 'All in RAM', 'All on disk', 'Disk + memory buffers'. Each runs a 10-second sim of 1 million enqueues/dequeues with a crash event at second 7: RAM is fastest but the crash wipes the frontier (counter drops to 0); disk survives but the throughput gauge crawls; hybrid stays fast and loses only the unflushed buffer (a small sliver).
stages.check: Lab A target beaten; Lab B all three run. Q.quiz with 2 questions: 'Two recrawl strategies?' → update history; importance-first/more often; 'Why not keep the whole frontier in memory?' → too big and lost on a crash (not durable, not scalable).

stages.title: Boss: The Frontier Warden
stages.sub: Which part of the frontier handles it?
stages.teaches: Mapping frontier problems to front queues, back queues, recrawl policy or storage.
stages.interaction: Q.boss with choices [{k:'front', label:'Front queues', sub:'priority'}, {k:'back', label:'Back queues', sub:'politeness'}, {k:'fresh', label:'Recrawl policy', sub:'freshness'}, {k:'store', label:'Frontier storage', sub:'memory + disk'}]. Scenarios (8): 'A small blog's owner complains about 20 requests per second from us' → back; 'The crawler spends its first week on spam forums while news sites wait' → front; 'Search results show prices from three months ago' → fresh; 'The frontier server restarted and 200 million URLs vanished' → store; 'Two worker threads were both downloading from apple.com at the same time' → back (one host, one queue, one worker); 'Low-priority URLs haven't been crawled in months' → front (strict priority starving: use biased random); 'Breaking-news homepages change every few minutes but we revisit them monthly' → fresh; 'Enqueues are blocked waiting on disk writes' → store (memory buffers, periodic flush).
stages.check: Boss cleared.

stages.title: Say it like a senior
stages.teaches: The deep-dive answer interviewers most often probe.
stages.interaction: Q.drill. Prompt: 'Your crawler is a BFS. What's wrong with that, and how does your URL frontier fix it?' Placeholder: 'BFS is the right start, but…'. Model: 'BFS beats DFS because the web is too deep for DFS, but plain BFS has two problems: most links point back to the same host, so we'd hammer it, and it treats every URL as equally important. So the frontier has two layers. Front queues handle priority: a prioritizer scores URLs by things like PageRank, traffic and update frequency and puts them in queues by priority, and a selector picks randomly but biased toward high priority so nothing starves. Back queues handle politeness: a router uses a host-to-queue mapping so each queue holds one host, each worker owns a queue, downloads one page at a time and waits between requests. For freshness I recrawl based on update history and recrawl important pages more often. The frontier is too big for memory, so it lives on disk with in-memory buffers for enqueue and dequeue.' Checks: ['I said why DFS is a poor fit and BFS has two problems', 'I described front queues with biased selection', 'I described back queues with host→queue mapping, one worker per queue, and delay', 'I covered freshness and disk + memory buffer storage'].
stages.check: Self-grade via Q.drill.

caveats: The book's figure shows one queue per host, but there are hundreds of millions of hosts. Mercator-style frontiers keep a bounded number of back queues (Mercator suggested about three times the number of crawler threads) and reassign them to new hosts as they empty.

Politeness is really per server, not per host name: thousands of small sites can share one IP on a hosting provider, so careful crawlers also limit by IP. Mercator also scaled the delay with how slow the host was (wait several times the last download time) rather than using a fixed pause.
'One page at a time per host' is conservative. Big sites can take more, and Google adjusts its crawl rate per site based on how fast and error-free the server is.
PageRank is the book's example signal; modern search engines use many signals and keep the details private. Treat the prioritizer as 'some scoring function', not a known algorithm.

Freshness research (Cho & Garcia-Molina) found a surprising result: revisiting pages strictly in proportion to how often they change can do worse than you'd expect, because pages that change constantly go stale again almost immediately. 'Recrawl what changes often' is a good first answer, not the last word.

quests.d: robots.txt, four speed-ups for the downloader (distribute, cache DNS, go local, time out), and four ways to survive failures
quests.goal: Your win today: you can explain robots.txt and why it's cached, name the four downloader optimisations with the DNS numbers (10–200 ms per lookup), and list the four robustness measures, including how consistent hashing spreads hosts across downloader servers.
quests.bookSections: Step 3 deep dive: HTML Downloader (Robots.txt, performance optimisation: distributed crawl, cache DNS resolver, locality, short timeout); Robustness (consistent hashing, save crawl states and data, exception handling, data validation)

stages.title: Read the house rules
stages.teaches: The HTML Downloader fetches pages over HTTP. Before crawling a site, a crawler should fetch that site's robots.txt (at the root, e.g. example.com/robots.txt) and obey it. The file tells crawlers which paths they may not download, grouped by User-agent (which bot the rules apply to) with Disallow lines (path prefixes, sometimes with wildcards). The book shows part of a large retailer's real robots.txt with Disallow rules for Googlebot. To avoid downloading robots.txt again before every page, the crawler caches it and refreshes the cached copy periodically.
stages.interaction: Rule-checker sim with a made-up file (not copied from any real site): 'User-agent: *  Disallow: /cart/  Disallow: /search  ·  User-agent: SpiderBot  Disallow: /private/  Allow: /private/press/'. On the right, 8 URL cards on shop.example: /products/42, /cart/checkout, /search?q=shoes, /private/hr, /private/press/launch, /blog/post-1, /searching-tips, /CART/x. A toggle chooses which bot we are ('SpiderBot' or 'OtherBot'). The learner marks each card Allowed or Blocked for the current bot, then presses 'Check'. Teaching moments: a bot that has its own group uses only that group, not the '*' group (so SpiderBot may fetch /cart/ here); '/search' as a prefix also blocks '/searching-tips'; paths are case-sensitive so '/CART/x' isn't blocked; Allow can carve out an exception (/private/press/). Finally a counter panel: 'Pages fetched from shop.example today: 50,000. robots.txt downloads without cache: 50,000; with a cache refreshed daily: 1.'
stages.check: All 8 cards correct for both bots (retries allowed). Answer key, SpiderBot (uses only its own group): Blocked = /private/hr; Allowed = everything else including /cart/checkout, /search?q=shoes and /private/press/launch. OtherBot (falls back to *): Blocked = /cart/checkout, /search?q=shoes, /searching-tips; Allowed = /products/42, /private/hr, /private/press/launch, /blog/post-1, /CART/x. Q.quiz with 2 questions: 'When must the crawler check robots.txt?' → before crawling a site; 'Why cache it?' → avoid re-downloading it for every page.

stages.title: Split the work
stages.teaches: To go fast, crawl jobs are spread over many servers, and each server runs many threads. The URL space is partitioned so each downloader handles its own subset of URLs. This is where scale comes from: the 400–800 pages/s target is far more than one thread could manage when each fetch takes hundreds of milliseconds.
stages.interaction: Throughput calculator + sim. Sliders: servers (1–50), threads per server (1–200), average fetch time (100 ms–2 s). A live readout: pages/s ≈ servers × threads ÷ fetch time. Goal markers at 400 (average) and 800 (peak). The learner must find two different settings that clear 800 pages/s with fetch time fixed at 1 s (e.g. 8 servers × 100 threads; 4 × 200). A small animation shows URL tiles being dealt to server lanes by hash of host, so all of a host's URLs land in the same lane (this foreshadows consistent hashing in stage 5).
stages.check: Two valid settings found. Q.quiz 1 question: 'Pages/s with 10 servers × 50 threads and 0.5 s per fetch?' → 1,000.

stages.title: Stop asking for directions
stages.sub: Speed-ups 2–4 · DNS cache, locality, short timeout
stages.teaches: Cache the DNS resolver: DNS is a bottleneck because many DNS interfaces are synchronous, so a lookup blocks, and a DNS answer takes roughly 10 ms to 200 ms. While one crawler thread waits on a lookup, other threads can be blocked too. Keeping a DNS cache (host name → IP) avoids most lookups; the book refreshes it periodically with cron jobs. Locality: place crawl servers in different regions so they're close to the sites they crawl; shorter distance means faster downloads. Locality applies to most parts of the system: crawl servers, cache, queue, storage. Short timeout: some servers answer very slowly or never. Set a maximum wait; if a host doesn't respond in time, give up on that page and crawl something else.
stages.interaction: Three-toggle race. A timeline view of 8 worker threads fetching 40 pages from a mix of hosts (some repeat hosts, a few far-away, two 'black hole' hosts that never answer). Three toggles: 'DNS cache', 'Regional crawlers', 'Timeout = 5 s'. Each segment of a thread's bar is coloured: DNS (purple), network round trip (blue), download (green), waiting on a dead host (grey). Before the learner turns anything on, they predict which single toggle will cut total time the most for this workload (choices: DNS / locality / timeout) → timeout (the two black-hole hosts freeze two threads for the whole run, the biggest chunk of grey). Then they flip toggles one at a time and the total time readout drops; with all three the bars become short and mostly green. A DNS side panel: 'Lookups without cache: 40; with cache: 9 (one per unique host).' Caption on DNS: 'a synchronous lookup blocks; caching removes the wait from most fetches'.
stages.check: Prediction made and all toggles tried. Q.quiz with 3 questions: 'Typical DNS response time per the book?' → 10–200 ms; 'Why does slow DNS hurt more than its own time?' → synchronous lookups can block other threads; 'A host hasn't answered in 30 s, what should the crawler do?' → time out and move on to other pages.

stages.title: Built to survive
stages.teaches: Four ways the book makes the crawler robust. (1) Consistent hashing spreads the load across downloader servers, so a server can be added or removed and only a small slice of hosts moves (callback to World 6). (2) Save crawl state and data: write the crawl's progress and data to storage, so a crashed or interrupted crawl restarts by loading the saved state instead of from scratch. (3) Exception handling: errors are normal on the web, so a bad page or a failed fetch must be caught and handled without crashing the whole system. (4) Data validation: check data at each step to stop bad input from causing system errors.
stages.interaction: Chaos-monkey panel. A running mini-crawl with 4 downloader servers drawn on a hash ring (hosts as dots on the ring). The learner presses chaos buttons and picks the defence that saves the day from 4 shield buttons before the outcome plays. 'Server D crashes' → consistent hashing: only D's arc of hosts moves to the next server clockwise (animated), others untouched; contrast toggle 'hash mod N' shows nearly every host reshuffling. 'Power cut to the whole cluster' → saved state: crawl resumes from the last checkpoint with a progress bar that keeps most of its fill. 'A page returns 3 MB of binary garbage labelled text/html' → exception handling: that one task fails, the worker logs and moves on. 'A URL field arrives as 9,000 characters of nonsense' → data validation: rejected at the door. Wrong shield shows what would have happened (e.g. the whole worker process dies).
stages.check: All 4 chaos events defended. Q.quiz with 2 questions: 'Removing one of 4 downloader servers with consistent hashing moves about what share of hosts?' → about a quarter (vs nearly all with mod N); 'What does saving crawl state buy you?' → restart from where you were after a failure.

stages.title: Boss: The Slow Web Gauntlet
stages.sub: Pick the fix for each slowdown or failure
stages.teaches: Choosing between robots.txt, the four speed-ups and the four defences.
stages.interaction: Q.boss with choices [{k:'robots', label:'robots.txt (cached)', sub:'house rules'}, {k:'speed', label:'Speed-up', sub:'distribute · DNS cache · locality · timeout'}, {k:'robust', label:'Robustness', sub:'hashing · checkpoints · exceptions · validation'}]. Scenarios (8): 'Profiling shows threads spend 40% of their time waiting on name lookups' → speed (DNS cache); 'A site owner says we crawled /admin/ pages they asked bots to avoid' → robots; 'We fetch robots.txt before every single page and it doubles our request count' → robots (cache it); 'Crawling Japanese sites from a US data centre is slow' → speed (locality); 'One downloader server is added and every host gets reassigned' → robust (consistent hashing); 'A week-long crawl crashed on day 6 and restarted from zero' → robust (save state); 'A few hosts never answer and tie up threads for minutes' → speed (short timeout); 'A malformed response kills the whole worker process' → robust (exception handling).
stages.check: Boss cleared.

stages.title: Say it like a senior
stages.teaches: Downloader plus robustness, compact.
stages.interaction: Q.drill. Prompt: 'How do you make the downloader fast without being rude, and what keeps it alive when things break?' Placeholder: 'First, it reads robots.txt…'. Model: 'Before crawling a site the downloader reads its robots.txt and obeys the disallowed paths; we cache that file and refresh it periodically so we don't fetch it per page. For speed: distribute the crawl over many servers with many threads each, partitioning URLs by host; cache DNS, because lookups take 10 to 200 milliseconds and are often synchronous, so they block threads; put crawlers in several regions close to the sites; and use short timeouts so dead servers don't tie up threads. For robustness: consistent hashing assigns hosts to downloader servers so adding or losing one only moves a slice; we checkpoint crawl state and data so a crash resumes instead of restarting; we handle exceptions per page so one bad response can't crash the system; and we validate data.' Checks: ['robots.txt checked first and cached', 'all four speed-ups, with the DNS 10–200 ms number', 'all four robustness measures', 'consistent hashing explained as moving only a slice'].
stages.check: Self-grade via Q.drill.

caveats: robots.txt is a convention, not a lock: well-behaved crawlers obey it, bad ones ignore it, and it does not hide pages from being linked or indexed by URL. It was only formally standardised in 2022 as RFC 9309, which also says crawlers should not cache it for more than 24 hours in general.
The common 'Crawl-delay' line is not part of the standard. Some crawlers honour it, and Google ignores it and sets its own rate based on how the server responds.

The book refreshes the DNS cache with cron jobs. Real resolvers respect each record's TTL (time-to-live) instead, and big crawlers often run their own asynchronous resolver; Mercator famously wrote a custom multi-threaded DNS resolver because the standard library call was synchronous.

'Short timeout' must be paired with retry and back-off: a host that timed out once might just be busy. Status codes like 429 (Too Many Requests) and 503 with a Retry-After header are the site asking you to slow down, which is politeness again.

Consistent hashing by host also keeps all of a host's URLs on one server, which is what makes per-host politeness enforceable in a distributed crawl. The book lists it under robustness, but it is equally a politeness tool.

quests.d: Plug-in modules for new content, dodging duplicates, spider traps and noise, and the wrap-up extras like rendering JavaScript
quests.goal: Your win today: you can show how a new module (PNG downloader, web monitor) plugs into the pipeline, name the three kinds of problematic content and how to handle each, explain why a spider trap needs a URL length limit plus human review, and list the wrap-up talking points.
quests.bookSections: Step 3 deep dive: Extensibility; Detect and avoid problematic content (redundant content, spider traps, data noise); Step 4: Wrap up (server-side rendering, filtering unwanted pages, database replication and sharding, horizontal scaling, availability/consistency/reliability, analytics)

stages.title: Snap-on modules
stages.teaches: Almost every system grows, so the crawler should accept new content types by plugging in new modules. The book's figure adds two: a PNG Downloader module beside the HTML downloader to fetch PNG images, and a Web Monitor module that watches the web for copyright and trademark infringement. The core loop (frontier, link extraction, seen-checks) stays the same; only a module is added at the right spot.
stages.interaction: Plug-the-socket puzzle. The pipeline diagram from 9.2 is shown with empty sockets at several points (beside the HTML Downloader; after Content Seen?; after the URL Filter). Three module tiles: 'PNG Downloader', 'Web Monitor', 'PDF Extractor' (bonus). The learner drags each to the socket where it belongs (PNG Downloader → beside HTML Downloader, fed by the URL filter letting .png through; Web Monitor → reads pages after Content Seen? and flags matches; PDF Extractor → beside the downloaders, like PNG). Plugging into the wrong socket animates a jam with a hint. After all are plugged, a 'changed code' meter shows only the new modules lit, the core untouched. Then one change request: 'Product now wants video thumbnails' → the learner picks which existing boxes must change from a checklist (answer: just the URL Filter rule and a new downloader module).
stages.check: All modules placed; change-request checklist correct. Q.quiz 1 question: 'What are the book's two example plug-in modules?' → PNG Downloader and Web Monitor.

stages.title: Into the spider trap
stages.sub: Infinite loops that look like pages
stages.teaches: A spider trap is a page or site that sends the crawler into an endless loop, for example an infinitely deep directory structure where /foo/bar/ links to /foo/bar/foo/bar/ and so on forever (the book's example is a made-up spidertrapexample site). One defence is a maximum URL length. But there's no one-size-fits-all answer. Traps are easy to spot by an unusually large number of pages found on one site, yet hard to catch with a fully automatic rule; a person can review the site and either exclude it or add a custom URL filter for it.
stages.interaction: Trap simulator. A crawler token enters a site with a hidden trap (a calendar page whose 'next month' link never ends, plus a /foo/bar recursion). A live counter shows pages found on this host per minute, and a URL ticker scrolls the URLs as they're generated (they get visibly longer and repetitive). Defence controls: 'Max URL length' slider (50–2,000 chars), 'Max pages per host' slider, and a 'Flag for human review' button that becomes active when the per-host page count crosses an anomaly line. Round 1: the /foo/bar trap. The learner sets max URL length; at ~200 chars the recursion is cut off. Round 2: the calendar trap, whose URLs stay short (/cal?month=2093-07): URL length doesn't help. Predict first: 'Will the URL length limit stop the calendar trap?' → no. The learner must use the per-host anomaly + human review (which adds a custom filter rule 'block /cal?month= beyond ±12 months'). Final screen: a legit giant site (a big encyclopedia with millions of real pages) also trips the anomaly line, and the reviewer correctly lets it through, showing why a human is in the loop.
stages.check: Both traps stopped and the prediction made. Q.quiz with 2 questions: 'Book's simple defence against deep-directory traps?' → maximum URL length; 'Why not auto-block every site with lots of pages?' → big legit sites have lots of pages too; the book says automatic detection is hard, so humans verify.

stages.title: Trash, twins and noise
stages.teaches: The book's three categories. Redundant content: nearly 30% of pages are duplicates; hashes or checksums detect them (the Content Seen? box). Spider traps: endless loops (previous stage). Data noise: content with little or no value, such as advertisements, code snippets and spam URLs; it doesn't help the crawl and should be excluded where possible. Wrap-up adds a related idea: with limited storage and crawl resources, an anti-spam component that filters low-quality and spam pages is worth having.
stages.interaction: Sorting conveyor. 12 items roll past on a belt, each a small 'page preview' card; the learner flicks each into one of four bins: Duplicate, Spider trap, Noise, Keep. Items include: the same press release on 5 mirror sites (Duplicate); /a/b/a/b/a/b/... (Trap); a page that is 95% ad blocks (Noise); a keyword-stuffed link farm (Noise / spam); a real news article (Keep); an endlessly paginated 'page=99999' archive (Trap); a printer-friendly copy of an article already stored (Duplicate); a 'download our toolbar' popup page (Noise); a well-written product review (Keep); a session-ID URL variant of a stored page (Duplicate); a tag cloud generating every combination of tags (Trap); a recipe page (Keep). Speed rises slowly; mistakes cost a heart only after the first 3 (warm-up).
stages.check: At least 10 of 12 correct. Q.quiz 1 question: 'Which tool catches redundant content?' → hashes/checksums (fingerprints).

stages.title: The page that builds itself
stages.sub: Wrap-up · rendering JavaScript and other extras
stages.teaches: Wrap-up talking points from the book: (1) Server-side rendering: many sites build links on the fly with JavaScript or AJAX, so downloading and parsing the raw HTML misses them; render the page first (run its scripts, also called dynamic rendering) and then parse. (2) Filter out unwanted pages with an anti-spam component. (3) Database replication and sharding for the data layer's availability, scalability and reliability. (4) Horizontal scaling: a large crawl needs hundreds or thousands of servers, and the key is keeping them stateless. (5) Availability, consistency and reliability, the general concerns of any large system. (6) Analytics: collect and analyse data to fine-tune the system.
stages.interaction:
Split-screen demo. Left: 'Raw HTML' view of a single-page app showing an almost empty body (
) and a script tag; the link extractor finds 0 links. Right: 'Rendered DOM' after pressing 'Run scripts' (a short animated spinner standing in for a headless browser): a menu and 6 product links appear, and the extractor finds 6. A cost meter shows rendering takes far more CPU and time per page (e.g. ~10× vs plain fetch, labelled illustrative). Then a pick-5 card round from 8 wrap-up cards, 'What would you raise in the last 3 minutes?': strong cards are the six book points above (any 5 accepted); weak cards: 'rewrite it in Rust', 'store pages on the blockchain'. Each pick gets a one-line interviewer reaction.
stages.check: Both views compared and 5 strong cards picked. Q.quiz with 2 questions: 'Why can a crawler miss links on a modern site?' → links are generated by JavaScript after load, so raw HTML doesn't contain them; 'Key to horizontal scaling of crawl servers?' → keep them stateless.

stages.title: Boss: The Trap Hydra
stages.sub: Duplicate, trap, noise, extension or rendering?
stages.teaches: Applying extensibility, problematic-content handling and wrap-up extras to realistic incidents.
stages.interaction: Q.boss with choices [{k:'dup', label:'Dedupe', sub:'hash / checksum'}, {k:'trap', label:'Trap guard', sub:'URL length, review, custom filter'}, {k:'noise', label:'Filter noise / spam', sub:'anti-spam'}, {k:'module', label:'Plug in a module', sub:'extensibility'}, {k:'render', label:'Render first', sub:'run the JavaScript'}]. Scenarios (8): 'One small site has produced 40 million URLs this week' → trap; 'A React shop shows zero product links in our index' → render; 'Legal wants alerts when our trademark appears on new sites' → module (web monitor); 'Storage is filling with pages that are 90% ads and keyword stuffing' → noise; 'The same syndicated article appears on 300 news sites' → dup; 'URLs like /x/y/x/y/x/y/x/y keep growing' → trap (max URL length); 'Image search launches next quarter' → module (PNG downloader); 'A link farm of thousands of auto-generated pages links to itself' → noise (spam filter) and mention it may also look like a trap.
stages.check: Boss cleared.

stages.title: Say it like a senior
stages.teaches: The tail end of the interview.
stages.interaction: Q.drill. Prompt: 'What problematic content will your crawler meet, how does it grow to new content types, and what would you add with more time?' Placeholder: 'Three kinds of bad content…'. Model: 'There are three kinds of bad content. Duplicates, close to a third of pages, which we catch by hashing page content. Spider traps, like infinitely deep URLs or endless calendars; a maximum URL length handles the simple ones, but there's no universal rule, so we watch for sites with an abnormal number of pages and have a person exclude them or add a custom filter. And noise like ads, code snippets and spam, which we filter out, ideally with an anti-spam component. For extensibility, new content types are plug-in modules, like a PNG downloader or a web-monitor for copyright, without touching the core loop. With more time: render JavaScript before parsing so we see dynamically generated links, replicate and shard the storage, keep crawl servers stateless so we can scale out to thousands, and add analytics.' Checks: ['I named duplicates, spider traps and noise with a fix for each', 'I said URL length helps but traps need detection plus human review', 'I gave a plug-in module example', 'I listed at least three wrap-up points including rendering'].
stages.check: Self-grade via Q.drill.

caveats: A maximum URL length only stops traps whose URLs grow. Calendars, session IDs and faceted search ('?color=red&size=9&sort=…') create endless URLs of normal length, so real crawlers also cap pages per host, cap link depth, and normalise or strip parameters.

The book calls it 'server-side rendering', but it means the crawler running the page's JavaScript itself (in a headless browser) before parsing. Google now renders JavaScript in its own crawler and describes 'dynamic rendering' (serving bots a pre-rendered version) as a workaround it no longer recommends.
Rendering is expensive: running a browser per page costs far more CPU and time than a plain fetch, so crawlers render selectively (often in a second, delayed pass) rather than for every page.

'Noise' is a judgement call: code snippets are noise for a general web index but exactly the content a code-search engine wants. What counts as noise depends on the crawler's purpose, which is why scoping comes first.

quests.d: Full mock interview: design a web crawler in 45 minutes
quests.goal: Your win today: you can run the whole interview without notes, from scoping and 400/800 pages/s and 30 PB, through the pipeline and workflow, the two-layer URL frontier, downloader speed-ups and robustness, to traps, extensibility and a clean wrap-up.
quests.bookSections: Whole chapter via the 4-step framework: Step 1 scope, traits, estimates; Step 2 components and workflow; Step 3 BFS vs DFS, URL frontier (politeness, priority, freshness, storage), HTML downloader (robots.txt, performance), robustness, extensibility, problematic content; Step 4 wrap up

stages.title: Scope it
stages.teaches: Requirements: search engine indexing; 1 billion pages/month; HTML only; pick up new and edited pages; store HTML up to 5 years; ignore duplicate content. Traits: scalability, robustness, politeness, extensibility. Estimates: ~400 pages/s, ~800 peak, 500 TB/month at 500 KB/page, 30 PB over 5 years.
stages.interaction: Interview chat UI like 0008: the interviewer bubble says 'Design a web crawler.' The learner has 6 'question tokens' and a deck of 11 questions (6 strong, 3 weak, 2 premature-implementation like 'Kafka or RabbitMQ?'). Strong picks get the interviewer's reply pinned to a requirement board; weak picks spend a token with a coach note. Then a 'traits' quick-pick (choose 4 of 7: scalable, robust, polite, extensible + distractors 'real-time', 'strongly consistent', 'serverless'). Then a rapid estimate round: 4 multiple-choice estimates (avg QPS, peak QPS, monthly storage, 5-year storage), each with 3 options within an order of magnitude and a 'show work' toggle.
stages.check: Board holds the 6 requirements, 4 traits picked, 4 estimates correct (retry allowed). Scorecard records wasted tokens.

stages.title: Sketch it
stages.sub: Step 2 · high-level design and buy-in (10–15 min)
stages.teaches: Seed URLs → URL Frontier → HTML Downloader (+ DNS Resolver) → Content Parser → Content Seen? (→ Content Storage) → URL Extractor → URL Filter → URL Seen? (→ URL Storage) → back to URL Frontier.
stages.interaction: Whiteboard builder: 14 tiles (the 11 real components plus distractors 'Load balancer for users', 'Redis pub/sub', 'GraphQL gateway') to drag onto a canvas and connect with arrows. Minimum correct: all 11 components wired in the right order, with storage boxes hanging off the two seen-checks and the loop closing back to the frontier. Distractors get a 'what's that for here?' note and don't block progress. Then the interviewer asks two buy-in questions inline: 'Why compare hashes in Content Seen?' and 'What would you use for URL Seen?' (choose from chips: Bloom filter / hash table / SQL LIKE query / linear scan; first two accepted, and choosing Bloom filter triggers 'and its downside?' → false positives skip some new URLs).
stages.check: Diagram has the 11 components wired correctly and both buy-in questions answered.

stages.title: Dig in
stages.teaches: BFS over DFS, but BFS alone is impolite and priority-blind; front queues (prioritizer, f1…fn, biased selector) + back queues (router, host→queue mapping, b1…bn, selector, one worker per queue, delay); freshness by update history and importance; frontier on disk with memory buffers; robots.txt checked first and cached; distributed crawl, DNS cache (10–200 ms lookups), locality, short timeouts; consistent hashing, saved state, exception handling, data validation.
stages.interaction: Three deep-dive panels the interviewer 'zooms into'. (a) Frontier: an empty two-layer frame; the learner drags 8 frontier parts into the front or back half, then answers 'Which half stops us hammering wikipedia.com?' (back). (b) Downloader: a 'slow crawl' profile chart (bars for DNS wait, far-away hosts, dead hosts, robots.txt refetches); the learner assigns a fix to each bar from chips (DNS cache, locality, short timeout, cache robots.txt). (c) Pushback round: the interviewer challenges two choices the learner made earlier, e.g. 'Your Bloom filter says a brand-new URL was seen; now what?' (accept small loss / size it for target false-positive rate) and 'One downloader host dies: whose URLs move?' (only its arc on the consistent-hash ring).
stages.check: All three panels answered; at least one accepted mitigation per pushback.

stages.title: Boss: the curveball barrage
stages.teaches: Failure and extension follow-ups across the whole design.
stages.interaction: Q.boss with choices [{k:'frontier', label:'Frontier fix', sub:'priority · politeness · freshness'}, {k:'download', label:'Downloader fix', sub:'robots · DNS · locality · timeout'}, {k:'robust', label:'Robustness fix', sub:'hashing · checkpoints · exceptions'}, {k:'content', label:'Content fix', sub:'dedupe · traps · noise · render'}]. Scenarios (10): 'A site owner emails that our bot is overloading their server' → frontier (back queues / delay); 'The crawler wastes its first month on spam forums' → frontier (prioritizer) and mention anti-spam; 'Half our fetch time is name lookups' → download (DNS cache); 'A crawl server crashes; on reboot the crawl starts from scratch' → robust (save state); 'Indexed product pages on JavaScript-heavy shops have no links' → content (render first); 'One host has produced 50M URLs in a day' → content (spider trap guard); 'We add 10 downloader servers and every host gets reassigned' → robust (consistent hashing); 'Stale news results: homepages revisited monthly' → frontier (freshness); 'Threads stuck for minutes on servers that never answer' → download (short timeout); 'The same syndicated story is being stored from 300 different news sites' → content (hash-based dedupe in Content Seen?).
stages.check: Boss cleared.

stages.title: Wrap it up
stages.teaches: Wrap-up: recap the four traits (scalable, polite, extensible, robust); then extras: server-side (dynamic) rendering, anti-spam filtering of unwanted pages, database replication and sharding, horizontal scaling with stateless servers, availability/consistency/reliability, analytics. Plus honest call-outs: exact hashes miss near-duplicates; Bloom false positives skip some URLs; politeness should also be per IP.
stages.interaction: Pick-5 from 10 wrap-up cards against a soft 30-second timer (running out only adds a scorecard note). Strong: render JavaScript before parsing; anti-spam filter; DB replication + sharding; stateless crawl servers for horizontal scaling; analytics; near-duplicate detection caveat; per-IP politeness caveat. Weak: 'rewrite in Rust', 'add a mobile app', 'switch to GraphQL'. The interviewer reacts to each pick.
stages.check: At least 4 strong picks.

stages.title: Say it like a senior
stages.teaches: The whole chapter as one answer.
stages.interaction: Q.drill. Prompt: 'You have 90 seconds. Summarise your web crawler design.' Model: 'Scope: a crawler for search indexing, a billion HTML pages a month, picking up new and changed pages, keeping the HTML five years and skipping duplicates. That's about 400 pages a second, 800 at peak, 500 TB a month and 30 PB over five years. It must be scalable, robust, polite and extensible. Pipeline: seed URLs feed the URL frontier; downloaders resolve DNS and fetch; a parser validates; Content Seen? hashes pages to drop duplicates; new pages are stored and their links extracted, made absolute, filtered, and checked against URL Seen?, a Bloom filter, before going back into the frontier. The frontier has front queues for priority, scored by things like PageRank and change rate with a biased random selector, and back queues for politeness: one host per queue, one worker per queue, a delay between requests. We recrawl by update history and importance, and keep the frontier on disk with memory buffers. Downloaders obey cached robots.txt, are distributed by consistent hashing on host, cache DNS, sit near the sites they crawl and use short timeouts. We checkpoint state, handle exceptions per page and validate data. We cap URL length and review abnormal sites for spider traps, filter noise and spam, plug in modules for new content types, and render JavaScript for dynamic sites.' Checks: ['Scope and the four estimates', 'Four traits', 'Full pipeline including both seen-checks', 'Front queues for priority and back queues for politeness', 'Downloader speed-ups and robustness measures', 'Traps, noise, extensibility and rendering']. After the drill, show a scorecard summarising tokens used, diagram accuracy, boss score and wrap-up picks, saved under a separate key 'sdq:v1:0906-interview' like 0008.
stages.check: Self-grade via Q.drill; scorecard shown.

caveats: The book's design is a teaching model built on Mercator-era ideas (late 1990s). Modern crawlers add JavaScript rendering pipelines, near-duplicate fingerprints, per-IP and adaptive rate limits, and machine-learned priority, but the skeleton (frontier, fetch, parse, dedupe, extract, filter, seen-check) is the same.

The interview prompt usually doesn't need indexing, ranking or search serving. Say explicitly that those are downstream consumers of Content Storage and out of scope, so the interviewer knows you know where the crawler ends.
Interviewers often probe one area hard (most commonly the URL frontier's politeness and priority). It's fine to skim the rest and go deep where they push.

cheatsheetOutline: Title: World 9, Design a Web Crawler (one page). §9.1 Scope & estimates: four uses (indexing, archiving, mining, monitoring); the 3-step loop (download → extract links → add new URLs, from seeds); requirements (search indexing, 1B pages/month, HTML only, new + edited pages, store 5 yrs, ignore duplicates); four traits (scalable, robust, polite, extensible); key numbers box (~400 pages/s avg [1B ÷ 2.6M s ≈ 386], ~800 peak at 2×, 500 KB/page → 500 TB/month, × 60 months = 30 PB). §9.2 Pipeline: diagram of the 11 boxes with one-line jobs; 11-step workflow; Content Seen? = hash pages, ~29% duplicates; URL Seen? = Bloom filter (no false negatives, false positives skip URLs) or hash table; sizing mini-table for 1B URLs (raw ~100 GB, 8-byte fingerprints ~8 GB, Bloom 1% ~1.2 GB); relative → absolute link example. §9.3 URL frontier: DFS too deep, BFS = FIFO but impolite + priority-blind; two-layer diagram (front: Prioritizer → f1…fn → biased random selector; back: router → host→queue mapping table → b1…bn → selector → workers, one page at a time + delay); priority signals (PageRank, traffic, update frequency); freshness (update history, important pages more often); storage (disk + in-memory enqueue/dequeue buffers). §9.4 Downloader & robustness: robots.txt (User-agent / Disallow / Allow, check first, cache, RFC 9309); four speed-ups (distributed crawl, DNS cache [10–200 ms lookups, synchronous], locality, short timeout); throughput formula servers × threads ÷ fetch time; four robustness measures (consistent hashing, save state/data, exception handling, data validation). §9.5 Traps & extensibility: plug-in modules (PNG Downloader, Web Monitor); problematic content (redundant → hash/checksum; spider traps → max URL length + per-host anomaly + human review/custom filter; data noise → exclude ads/snippets/spam); wrap-up extras (render JavaScript, anti-spam, DB replication + sharding, stateless horizontal scaling, availability/consistency/reliability, analytics). Final design diagram: Seed URLs → URL Frontier (front queues for priority, back queues for politeness, disk + buffers) → distributed HTML Downloaders (robots.txt cache, DNS cache, regional, timeouts, consistent hashing by host) → Content Parser → Content Seen? ↔ Content Storage → URL Extractor → URL Filter → URL Seen? ↔ URL Storage → back to the frontier, with plug-in module sockets. Footer: 'What happens when…?' quick answers (host overloaded → back queues/delay; spam first → prioritizer; slow DNS → cache; server dies → consistent hashing + checkpoints; JS sites → render; one host explodes → trap guard; 10× scale → stateless servers, ~4,000 pages/s). Caveats strip: near-duplicates need shingling/SimHash; politeness per IP; robots.txt is voluntary and Crawl-delay is non-standard; book's 'server-side rendering' means the crawler renders.
